title: IRQ Imbalance Across CPU Cores
exclusions: Measures the distribution of increments in cumulative counters for numeric hardware-IRQ rows in `/proc/interrupts` across online CPUs. It excludes nonnumeric pseudo-vectors such as NMI, LOC, RES, CAL, and TLB; software interrupts; IRQ service time; per-device latency; and root-cause attribution. A concentrated count does not by itself prove CPU saturation or a fault: queue affinity, NUMA locality, isolated CPUs, and real-time tuning can make concentration intentional. Only unexpired CPU exclusions in `linux_irq_core_scope.csv` affect the SPL. The use case does not alter affinity, verify that `irqbalance` is effective, or provide regulatory evidence.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_irq_core_concentration_10m` saved-search definition, scheduler and alert history, the versioned `linux_irq_core_scope.csv` lookup, and a dashboard export containing `_time`, `host`, `busiest_cpu`, `busiest_core_interrupts`, `total_interrupts`, `busiest_core_share_pct`, `equal_share_pct`, `concentration_ratio`, `included_core_count`, and `scoped_out_core_count`. These artifacts show collector and search results; they are not production validation, root-cause proof, or compliance attestation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a temporary index with no active scope exclusions, create 60-second `linux:irq_count` samples for `host=irq-positive`, CPUs 0-3, one fixed `boot_id`, and `numeric_irq_vectors=32`. Across each of two consecutive complete five-minute buckets, increment `cumulative_hardirq_count` by 3000 per minute on CPU0 and 100 per minute on each other CPU. Each bucket then has 16500 interrupts, CPU0 has 15000 (90.91%), equal share is 25%, and `concentration_ratio` is 3.64. Run the SPL with `now()` aligned after the second bucket and expect exactly one row for `irq-positive` with `busiest_cpu=0`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Create the same two-bucket sequence for `host=irq-balanced`, but increment every CPU by 1000 per minute. Each bucket has 20000 interrupts, each CPU has 5000, and `concentration_ratio=1`; expect zero rows. Also rerun the positive sequence with an unexpired lookup row `irq-positive,0,0,<future_epoch>,authorized RT isolation`; CPU0 must be scoped out and the alert must return zero rows because the remaining total is below 10000.

dataSources: A locally managed Splunk Universal Forwarder scripted input reads `/proc/interrupts` every 60 seconds and writes newline-delimited JSON to the deployment-selected `index=os` with the local convention `sourcetype=linux:irq_count`. It emits one event per online CPU with required fields `sample_epoch`, `boot_id`, `cpu_id`, `cumulative_hardirq_count`, and `numeric_irq_vectors`; `host` is Splunk metadata. The counter is the sum, for that CPU, of all numeric IRQ rows visible in the file. Neither this sourcetype nor these fields are supplied by the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder native scripted input packaged in a locally managed `linux_irq_input` deployment app. No Splunkbase add-on is required; the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) does not document a `/proc/interrupts` collector.
spl:
index=os sourcetype="linux:irq_count" earliest=-16m@m latest=@m
| fields _time host sample_epoch boot_id cpu_id cumulative_hardirq_count numeric_irq_vectors
| eval sample_epoch=tonumber(sample_epoch), cpu_id=tonumber(cpu_id), cumulative_hardirq_count=tonumber(cumulative_hardirq_count), numeric_irq_vectors=tonumber(numeric_irq_vectors)
| where isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(sample_epoch) AND isnotnull(cpu_id) AND isnotnull(cumulative_hardirq_count) AND isnotnull(numeric_irq_vectors)
| eval _time=sample_epoch
| bin _time span=1m
| stats latest(cumulative_hardirq_count) as cumulative_hardirq_count latest(numeric_irq_vectors) as numeric_irq_vectors latest(boot_id) as boot_id by _time host cpu_id
| sort 0 host cpu_id _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(cumulative_hardirq_count) as previous_count last(numeric_irq_vectors) as previous_vectors last(boot_id) as previous_boot_id last(_time) as previous_time by host cpu_id
| eval hardirq_delta=if(boot_id=previous_boot_id AND numeric_irq_vectors=previous_vectors AND cumulative_hardirq_count>=previous_count AND _time-previous_time>=30 AND _time-previous_time<=120,cumulative_hardirq_count-previous_count,null())
| where isnotnull(hardirq_delta)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats sum(hardirq_delta) as core_interrupts count as valid_intervals by _time host cpu_id
| lookup linux_irq_core_scope.csv host cpu_id OUTPUT include_cpu expires_epoch scope_reason
| eval include_cpu=if(tonumber(include_cpu)=0 AND tonumber(expires_epoch)>=now(),0,1)
| eventstats dc(cpu_id) as observed_core_count count(eval(include_cpu=0)) as scoped_out_core_count by _time host
| where include_cpu=1 AND valid_intervals>=4
| eventstats sum(core_interrupts) as total_interrupts count as included_core_count by _time host
| eval core_share_pct=100*core_interrupts/total_interrupts
| sort 0 host _time -core_interrupts cpu_id
| stats first(cpu_id) as busiest_cpu first(core_interrupts) as busiest_core_interrupts first(core_share_pct) as busiest_core_share_pct first(total_interrupts) as total_interrupts first(included_core_count) as included_core_count first(observed_core_count) as observed_core_count first(scoped_out_core_count) as scoped_out_core_count by _time host
| eval equal_share_pct=100/included_core_count, concentration_ratio=busiest_core_share_pct/equal_share_pct
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) as previous_bucket last(total_interrupts) as previous_total_interrupts last(included_core_count) as previous_included_core_count last(concentration_ratio) as previous_concentration_ratio by host
| eval latest_complete_epoch=floor(now()/300)*300-300
| where _time=latest_complete_epoch AND _time-previous_bucket=300 AND included_core_count>=2 AND previous_included_core_count>=2 AND total_interrupts>=10000 AND previous_total_interrupts>=10000 AND concentration_ratio>=3 AND previous_concentration_ratio>=3
| eval busiest_core_share_pct=round(busiest_core_share_pct,2), equal_share_pct=round(equal_share_pct,2), concentration_ratio=round(concentration_ratio,2), previous_concentration_ratio=round(previous_concentration_ratio,2)
| table _time host busiest_cpu busiest_core_interrupts total_interrupts busiest_core_share_pct equal_share_pct concentration_ratio previous_concentration_ratio included_core_count observed_core_count scoped_out_core_count
description: Reports one row per Linux host when the busiest included CPU handles at least three times its equal-share portion of numeric hardware-interrupt increments in each of two consecutive complete five-minute buckets, with at least 10,000 interrupts and two valid included CPUs in both buckets. The result identifies the busiest CPU and reports counts, percentages, core coverage, and concentration ratios.
value: Detecting sustained interrupt concentration helps platform teams correct a stopped or misconfigured balancing service, unintended affinity, or overloaded queue before interrupt handling contributes to packet loss, storage latency, or uneven application performance. Host, core, load volume, and concentration ratio improve focused investigation.
implementation: Deploy the exact `linux_irq_input` collector at a 60-second interval, verify its per-CPU cumulative totals against `/proc/interrupts`, and create the expiring CPU-scope lookup before saving the search. Schedule the search every five minutes. Start with the documented 10000-interrupt volume floor and 3.0-times-equal-share threshold sustained for ten minutes, then tune by hardware class and approved affinity design; never treat these catalogue defaults as vendor limits.
visualization: Use a host-by-CPU heatmap of five-minute `core_interrupts` with a count-based color scale, plus an alert table showing the busiest CPU, total interrupts, busiest-core share, equal share, concentration ratio, valid core count, and scoped-out core count. Add a 24-hour line chart of `concentration_ratio` by host and a separate collection-freshness panel. Label percentages as shares of counted numeric hardware IRQs, not CPU utilization.
dataModelAcceleration: The Splunk CIM Performance data model has CPU utilization fields but no normalized per-CPU `/proc/interrupts` cumulative hardware-IRQ counter. There is no equivalent CIM `tstats` search for this calculation; use the documented local fields unless the deployment owns and validates a custom data model.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Intentional queue or NUMA affinity** — A NIC or storage driver can assign each queue IRQ to a particular CPU, and `irqbalance` itself can isolate high-volume sources to preserve cache locality. Compare the busiest CPU with `/proc/irq/<irq>/smp_affinity_list`, device queue names in `/proc/interrupts`, NUMA topology, and the approved performance design before declaring a fault.

2. **Real-time or isolated CPUs** — `isolcpus`, `nohz_full`, tuned profiles, and `IRQBALANCE_BANNED_CPULIST` can intentionally remove CPUs from interrupt handling. Add only those explicitly approved host/CPU pairs to `linux_irq_core_scope.csv` with an owner, reason, and expiry; do not suppress the whole host.

3. **Workload dominated by one active queue** — A single-flow network test, storage benchmark, backup, or failover can legitimately drive one queue and therefore one CPU even while affinity is correct. Correlate with the named test or change, per-queue traffic, CPU IRQ time, packet loss, and latency; use a bounded change window rather than a permanent exclusion.

4. **CPU hotplug or IRQ-vector churn** — CPU online/offline operations and driver reloads change the CPU columns or numeric vector count. The SPL rejects comparisons when `numeric_irq_vectors` changes and requires at least four valid intervals, but reduced core coverage can still be operationally significant. Check `observed_core_count`, `included_core_count`, kernel logs, and collector freshness before paging.

5. **Boot or irqbalance settling period** — Immediately after startup, drivers create vectors and `irqbalance` may move affinities while workload ramps. Verify a stable boot ID, vector count, and service state, then require the two complete windows already enforced by the search. If local policy permits startup suppression, scope it to the host's actual boot/change window and retain the raw result.

**Suppression mechanism:** create the `lookup linux_irq_core_scope.csv` with headers `host,cpu_id,include_cpu,expires_epoch,scope_reason`. The SPL honors only `include_cpu=0` rows whose numeric UTC `expires_epoch` is still in the future; missing, malformed, and expired rows default to included. Require an accountable owner in the accompanying change record, review exclusions regularly, and never use a wildcard host or nonexpiring entry.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement contract

Deploy a Splunk Universal Forwarder on each Linux host and a local deployment app named `linux_irq_input`; this app and `linux:irq_count` are site conventions, not Splunkbase products. The forwarder account needs read access to `/proc/interrupts` and `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`, which should be tested directly without granting sudo. Select an operating-system event index and grant the operations search role access. This record uses `index=os`; change both the input and SPL if the approved local index differs.

`/proc/interrupts` exposes one counter column for each online CPU. The collector deliberately includes only rows whose label before the colon is a decimal IRQ number. It sums those cumulative counters per CPU and does not include architecture-specific pseudo-vectors such as NMI, LOC, RES, CAL, or TLB. The resulting value is a count since the relevant kernel/IRQ lifetime, not a rate, duration, percentage, or CPU-utilization value. The SPL derives increments between polls and rejects a reboot, a counter decrease, a changed numeric-vector count, or an implausible sample gap.

## 1. Install the exact collector

Create `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_irq_input/bin/collect_irq_counts.py`, owned by the forwarder account and executable, with this complete Python 3 body:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import re
import time
from pathlib import Path

lines = Path("/proc/interrupts").read_text(encoding="ascii").splitlines()
if not lines:
    raise SystemExit("/proc/interrupts is empty")
cpus = [int(value) for value in re.findall(r"CPU([0-9]+)", lines[0])]
if not cpus:
    raise SystemExit("no CPU columns found in /proc/interrupts")
totals = [0] * len(cpus)
numeric_irq_vectors = 0
for line in lines[1:]:
    if ":" not in line:
        continue
    irq_text, payload = line.split(":", 1)
    if not irq_text.strip().isdigit():
        continue
    fields = payload.split()
    counts = fields[:len(cpus)]
    if len(counts) != len(cpus) or any(not value.isdigit() for value in counts):
        continue
    numeric_irq_vectors += 1
    for position, value in enumerate(counts):
        totals[position] += int(value)
if numeric_irq_vectors == 0:
    raise SystemExit("no numeric IRQ rows found")
boot_id = Path("/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id").read_text(encoding="ascii").strip()
sample_epoch = int(time.time())
for cpu_id, total in zip(cpus, totals):
    print(json.dumps({
        "sample_epoch": sample_epoch,
        "boot_id": boot_id,
        "cpu_id": cpu_id,
        "cumulative_hardirq_count": total,
        "numeric_irq_vectors": numeric_irq_vectors
    }, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True))
```

This summary design emits one small JSON event per online CPU per minute rather than one event per IRQ/CPU pair. It is therefore suitable for distribution monitoring but cannot identify the responsible device by itself; the runbook returns to the raw file for that step.

Enable the script in `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_irq_input/local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_irq_input/bin/collect_irq_counts.py]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
source = proc_interrupts_summary
sourcetype = linux:irq_count
```

On the parsing tier, set `[linux:irq_count]` with `SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false`. On the search tier, set the same stanza in `props.conf` with `KV_MODE = json`. Do not also set `INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS = JSON`, because Splunk documents that combining it with `KV_MODE=json` extracts fields twice. The Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux may remain installed for other telemetry, but its documented scripts and source types do not replace this collector.

## 2. Verify source output and field semantics

Run the script as the forwarder service account. It must produce exactly one line for each `CPU<n>` header in `/proc/interrupts`, all lines must share one `sample_epoch`, `boot_id`, and `numeric_irq_vectors`, and every cumulative count must be a nonnegative integer. Independently sum the numeric IRQ columns on one representative host and compare them with the corresponding JSON values. A small difference is acceptable only if interrupts advanced between reads; the collector value must never be interpreted as interrupt time.

Use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on the forwarder to confirm the winning stanza, interval, index, source, and sourcetype. Then search `index=os sourcetype="linux:irq_count" earliest=-5m | table _time host sample_epoch boot_id cpu_id cumulative_hardirq_count numeric_irq_vectors`. Confirm approximately five samples per online CPU, increasing or unchanged cumulative values, stable vector counts during ordinary operation, JSON field extraction, and unique `host` identity. Stop rollout if different machines share one host value or if a script invocation omits only some CPUs.

Create `linux_irq_core_scope.csv` before saving the primary search. Use headers `host,cpu_id,include_cpu,expires_epoch,scope_reason`; a header-only file means no exclusions. An exclusion must identify one exact host and CPU, set `include_cpu` to `0`, carry a future UTC epoch expiry, and link through `scope_reason` to an approved real-time, isolation, or affinity decision. The SPL treats every other row as included.

## 3. Save, schedule, and tune the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_irq_core_concentration_10m` and schedule it every five minutes. Its 16-minute event lookback supplies a prior one-minute sample for both complete five-minute buckets. After replacing event time with the collector's `sample_epoch`, `streamstats current=f window=1` attaches the preceding per-host/per-CPU counter. A delta is valid only across the same boot and vector count, with a 30-120 second gap and no counter decrease. Each core needs four valid intervals in a bucket, allowing one missed poll while avoiding conclusions from sparse data.

For each complete bucket, the search divides the busiest included core's share by the equal share `100/included_core_count`. A ratio of 3.0 means the busiest core handled three times the count it would have handled under an even distribution; it does not mean 300% CPU utilization. The initial gate also requires at least 10000 counted interrupts per five minutes, at least two included CPUs, and a ratio of 3.0 or more in the current and immediately preceding bucket. Thus the condition is sustained for ten minutes. These are catalogue starting values chosen to reduce low-volume noise, not thresholds published by Linux, irqbalance, or Splunk. Baseline ratios by server model, CPU count, NIC/storage queue design, NUMA layout, and workload, then change the volume floor or ratio under normal search change control.

Create a result-count alert from the report. Trigger once when results are greater than zero and deduplicate incident actions by `host,busiest_cpu` for no longer than the investigation interval; keep each scheduled result in search history. Do not automate writes to `/proc/irq/*/smp_affinity` from this alert.

## 4. Validate logic without claiming runtime proof

Run both control scenarios in a temporary index using the same sourcetype and JSON extraction. Generate eleven timestamped samples per CPU so two complete five-minute buckets each have five deltas and the first sample supplies the boundary comparison. Keep `boot_id` and `numeric_irq_vectors` constant. The skewed fixture must return one current-bucket row with a 16500 count total, 90.91% busiest share, 25% equal share, and 3.64 ratio in both windows. The balanced fixture must return none. Add the expiring CPU0 scope row and verify that the positive fixture no longer passes the volume floor. Also test a changed boot ID, a lower cumulative count, a changed vector count, and a gap above 120 seconds; each boundary delta must be discarded.

On an authorized lab host, compare dashboard deltas with two timestamped copies of `/proc/interrupts`, inspect the CPU header, and verify `systemctl status irqbalance` plus `irqbalance --debug` according to local support practice. Record search job IDs and host-side captures if this runtime test is performed. This editorial review has not executed those tests and does not justify `status=verified`.

## 5. Respond, visualize, and troubleshoot

When a row fires, first confirm `included_core_count` matches the intended interrupt-handling CPU set and that collection is fresh. Inspect the busiest CPU's increasing rows in `/proc/interrupts`, map IRQ labels to NIC or storage queues, and read `/proc/irq/<irq>/smp_affinity_list`. Check whether `irqbalance` is active, whether the IRQ or CPU is banned, whether CPU isolation is configured, and whether a policy script or manual affinity owns the placement. Correlate with per-CPU `%irq`/`%soft`, device throughput, packet loss, storage latency, and kernel/driver changes. Escalate only when concentration conflicts with the approved design or accompanies impact. Let the platform or hardware owner change affinity; a blind attempt to make every IRQ equal can defeat NUMA and cache-locality tuning.

If no events arrive, execute the script as the forwarder user and inspect `splunkd.log` for `ExecProcessor` errors, Python availability, routing, and index permissions. If raw JSON exists but fields are absent, confirm `KV_MODE=json` on the search tier and the exact sourcetype spelling. If deltas are always null, inspect boot IDs, vector-count stability, counter direction, and sample gaps before changing the search. If a host disappears from results, use a freshness search rather than interpreting silence as balance. If `observed_core_count` exceeds `included_core_count`, distinguish explicit scope rows from cores rejected for insufficient valid intervals. Keep the heatmap and freshness panel adjacent so operators can see that an apparently quiet core may actually be missing data.
grandmaExplanation: We watch whether one processor is handling far more hardware signals than the others for a sustained period. That helps the team investigate uneven work before it contributes to network, storage, or server slowdowns.
